items.title: Ted Piltzecker interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 10, 2019
items.q: I came up with — I listened to Bill Evans and Clark Terry and you know, what do I know about this stuff.

ctx.x: Right. The Center for Arts in Education used to be called Lincoln Center Institute years ago. And my wife, who is a modern dancer, is still working for them. She was one of the first pioneers at that, and I came in and did a few years’ work with them. But she just breathes these concepts. And I’ve learned a lot. I’ve gone to a zillion dance concerts. It’s all the same, but yes I did do that kind of work and I love it. And there was a subsidiary in Lincoln, Nebraska called the Lead Institute, the Lead Center. And…

and in a certain sense directed a lot of my compositional thinking and sometimes my soloing too. And also it saved my tail when I became a composition professor because I wrote through a department called Studio Composition. And most of my constituents, certainly in the beginning, were singers, songwriters, rock & roll, indie bands, movie scoring people, people who write for video games you know. And so what do I know? I don’t know. I came up with — I listened to Bill Evans and Clark Terry and you know, what do I…

I totally agree and I learned so much from working with like — I had the same exact scenario working with classroom teachers. And there’s nothing like getting their — the questions they ask or the — like I remember doing a thing one day and I kept using the word “melody.” Finally, bless her heart, some teacher said, like, excuse me but, “What’s a melody?” And it was like this, oh man, this realization, that, find a way to not just use your own lingo. And boy that was very valuable.
